newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Little EU support for OECD ship deal without U.S.
newsitem.headline: Little EU support for OECD ship deal without U.S.

text.p: The European Union is not likely to steam ahead and implement an OECD accord to slash worldwide shipbuilding subsidies without the participation of the United States, EU officials said on Tuesday.

EU industry ministers will on Thursday start a sensitive debate on what the 15-nation bloc should do if Washington fails to ratify the deal struck in 1994 within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

While the EU still hopes the United States will succeed in securing approval for the accord in the Republican-controlled Congress, there is a growing awareness about the need to explore alternatives if this does not happen.
"The entry into force of the OECD agreement must remain the priority for the EU," a European Commission paper said.

"However, due to the uncertainty as to when this might take place it would be prudent to reflect on options for any future state aid regime in the absence of an OECD agreement, taking into account international developments," it added.

The working document, which will be presented to EU industry ministers meeting in Luxembourg, outlined various policy options, ranging from implementing the deal without the United States to rolling over existing EU ship aid rules.

EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann last month said the OECD accord, which was supposed to enter into force already at the start of 1996, could go forward without the United States if the EU, South Korea and Japan were aboard.
But EU officials said only a few EU member countries, notably the three Nordic member states, may be willing to favour such a way forward.
"It is not a realistic solution. It would not be possible to get a majority for that," one diplomat said.

Other options would be to extend the present aid rules for the sector, which allow for up to nine percent of contract related aid, or to agree on new EU legislation which would introduce stricter state support rules.

One diplomat said a majority of member states may be able to support the latter approach even if France and Mediterranean EU countries would prefer to first prolong the present regime for up to three more years after it expires by the end of 1997.
The shipbuilding sector is the only European manufacturing industry which still receives substantial amounts of operating aid as a result of the severe crisis in the 1970s and the 1980s.
The EU industry, still in difficulties due to depressed world prices, has gone through tough restructuring, slashing the workforce and capacity by more than half since 1976.
EU diplomats stress that the preferred alternative of all member states is that the United States ratifies the OECD deal and that it enters into force as soon as possible.

Those countries critical of state aid fear that an expected decision by EU industry ministers on Thursday to give the green light for restructuring aid to ailing German, Greek and Spanish shipyards would therefore send the wrong signal to Washington.
One EU diplomat said it may give the United States a good reason not to ratify the OECD deal. But the European Commission disputes this view, saying it should not be an obstacle.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky has expressed "dismay" at the proposal by the EU executive, questioning how the proposed aid would fit with commitments under the OECD deal.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert dismissed the criticism, noting that the EU, unlike the United States, had ratified the OECD deal in time and that the three restructuring cases were agreed before the OECD deal was signed.

Despite the opposition of Finland, Sweden, Denmark and Britain, most EU industry ministers are expected to back the European Commission's proposal to approve the requests of Bonn, Athens and Madrid to grant the state support to the yards.
